Additionally, Allen-Cahn experiments show that PI-SUPNs achieve lower solution and derivative errors at reduced computational cost, with more favorable loss landscapes than competing architectures. We also establish quasi-local approximation properties and spline-based convergence bounds for SUPNs. Our results show that shallow network architectures are an important mechanism for improving physics-informed trainability, but accurate solutions to the most challenging PDEs can still require FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization.
item.dc:creator: Zachary Morrow, Yucheng Fu, Pratanu Roy, Michael Penwarden

item.title: A Generalized Framework for Structured Low-Rank Approximation and Completion
item.description: arXiv:2611.28439v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We formulate a generalized version of SLRA, consisting of general affine constraints, which subsumes the problems of structured low-rank matrix approximation and completion as special cases. We characterize its critical points and propose an algorithm to approximately solve the general problem. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm for stock-price forecasting, computing approximate gcd of polynomials with noisy coefficients, and time-series denoising.
item.dc:creator: Rishav Chakraborty, A. Sanand Amita Dilip, Swanand R. Khare

item.title: Accelerating wave-scattering simulations with learned search directions
item.description: arXiv:2611.28499v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wave-scattering simulation requires solving a dense boundary-element system for every frequency, incidence and design. Krylov solvers build each search space from scratch, and it grows with problem size. Here we present BEMFormer, a solver that learns to generate search directions across systems of one integral equation and supplies geometry-specific directions through a coarse-grid correction. BEMFormer generalizes to unseen geometries, meshes and excitations, and to acoustic scattering after fine-tuning on eight geometries. It reproduces the measured radar cross-sections of benchmark targets. On a quadcopter with 1.04 million unknowns, 38 times the largest training problem, BEMFormer solves each system 30 times faster than a preconditioned Krylov solver. Both reach a radar cross-section deviation of about 1 dB, comparable to the difference between independent measurements and acceptable for engineering applications. These results show that solving million-unknown scattering problems in minutes is possible when the search space is learned rather than built from scratch.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Sun, Tao Shan, Hongyu Zhou, Rui Guo, Shenheng Xu, Fan Yang, Maokun Li

item.title: JAX-Nano: A GPU-Accelerated Differentiable Phonon Boltzmann Transport Solver for Nanoscale Heat Transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.28926v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As semiconductor device dimensions approach phonon mean free paths, heat transport enters ballistic and quasi-ballistic regimes where Fourier's law becomes inadequate. The phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) describes these nonequilibrium effects but presents significant computational challenges. This work introduces JAX-Nano, a GPU-accelerated, end-to-end differentiable phonon BTE solver for nanoscale heat transport. The solver integrates steady-state and transient BTE formulations within a unified finite-volume framework, supporting structured and unstructured meshes, mode-resolved transport, phonon scattering, volumetric heat generation, and multiple boundary conditions. Automatic differentiation enables gradient computation with respect to transport properties, boundary conditions, heat-generation rates, and geometric parameters without separately derived adjoint equations. Numerical predictions are validated against analytical solutions and established BTE solvers across diffusive-to-ballistic regimes. Applications to complex three-dimensional geometries are demonstrated using single-fin, double-fin, and arrayed fin field-effect transistor (FinFET) configurations. Gradient-based inverse learning enables single- and multi-parameter identification, including simultaneous recovery of mode-resolved phonon relaxation times and spatially distributed heat-generation rates in steady-state and transient problems. GPU performance and scalability are evaluated with respect to spatial resolution, angular discretization, and phonon bands, including comparisons with an MPI-based BTE solver. JAX-Nano provides a unified computational framework for three-dimensional phonon transport, automatic differentiation, and inverse parameter identification, enabling sensitivity analysis and optimization of nanoscale thermal systems.
item.dc:creator: Bo Zhang, Amy Zhaomei Zhang

item.title: Convergence analysis of resonant frequency approximation in periodic Helmholtz problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.29023v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate resonant frequencies of the Helmholtz equation in periodic structures under quasi-periodic conditions, using approximations of the associated quasi-periodic Green function, which is represented by a lattice sum. By formulating the periodic Helmholtz problem using layer potential operators whose kernel is given by the quasi-periodic Green function, resonant frequencies correspond to characteristic values of an associated operator-valued function. Based on two approximation methods for the quasi-periodic Green function, the Ewald method and the shifted Green function method, we propose the corresponding approximation schemes for resonant frequencies. Furthermore, we establish convergence rates for the resulting approximations using Gohberg--Sigal theory, where the Ewald method yields exponential convergence, while the shifted Green function method yields algebraic convergence. Numerical computations are presented to validate and compare the proposed approximation schemes.
item.dc:creator: Jiho Hong, Woojoo Lee, Mikyoung Lim

item.title: A shock-fitting approach to high-order simulation of viscous hypersonic flows based on inviscid implicit shock tracking
item.description: arXiv:2611.29564v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work presents a framework for computing viscous, shock-dominated flows at high Mach and Reynolds numbers in which the bow shock is located by inviscid implicit shock tracking and then treated as a boundary of the viscous computation. The high-order implicit shock tracking (HOIST) method is applied to the Euler equations on a coarse, shock-agnostic mesh to produce a shock-aligned mesh and the shock geometry; the elements upstream of the shock are discarded, the post-shock domain is remeshed to resolve the boundary layer, and the compressible Navier-Stokes equations are solved on it with a high-order interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method, with the post-shock state prescribed along the shock boundary by the oblique shock relations. Because the shock structure is never resolved, the approach requires neither the extreme element compression nor the specialized formulations that fully coupled viscous shock tracking demands at these conditions; the tracking optimization is confined to the coarse inviscid mesh, and the viscous computation involves no mesh unknowns and no additional nonlinear stabilization. The framework is demonstrated on a Mach 10.6 axisymmetric blunt cone, a Mach 17.6 cylinder, and a Mach 5 sphere in three dimensions, with surface pressure and heat flux in good agreement with experimental measurements and reference computations.
item.dc:creator: Huijing Dong, Alexander M. Perez Reyes, Matthew J. Zahr

item.title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.29922v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations by penalizing their residual, but this formulation can be difficult to optimize for solutions with singular behaviour. We focus specifically on the two-dimensional Laplace equation, whose strong analytical structure allows the governing equation to be enforced directly in the neural representation. We compare a hybrid harmonic-neural model with a holomorphic neural network whose output is harmonic by construction and therefore requires only boundary training. We further enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions chosen according to the interior angle and boundary conditions at each junction of boundary segments. On six singular benchmarks, the enriched model is the most accurate of the neural models we compare. On the four with a closed-form solution, however, that solution lies in the span of the enrichment terms, and a least-squares fit of these terms alone is exact to rounding error. On Motz's problem and the cracked beam, the neural core reduces the relative error of the recovered leading singular coefficient from about $10^{-2}$, for a least-squares fit with the same four terms, to about $10^{-6}$, and on four variants whose solution has a smooth part outside the span, the network is $4\times10^{4}$ to $2\times10^{7}$ times more accurate than a fit of its singular terms alone; classical least-squares fits with more singular terms, or with harmonic polynomials and rational poles, are more accurate still. Our results demonstrate how exploiting problem-specific analytical structure can provide an alternative to base and residual PINNs for challenging scientific computing problems.
item.dc:creator: Andrei Vlad Nicula, Kalp Shah, Robert-Stefan Sofroni, Mihnea Andrei B\^arsan, Agneya Bhardwaj, Jan Jel\'inek, Chris Hoes, Remco Hogerwerf, Finn Govers, Storm Koper, Gerrit Janssen, Stef de Wildt, Alejandro Valverde Mahou

item.title: IADR: Interface-Augmented Neural Operator for Phase-Field Mean-Curvature Flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.30153v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Allen-Cahn equation is one of the standard phase-field models for mean-curvature flow (MCF), parameterised by the diffuse-interface width $\varepsilon$. Practical simulations span a range of $\varepsilon$, so a single model covering this range is needed. PDE-specific neural operators are accurate but must be retrained at every $\varepsilon$; general neural operators cover $\varepsilon$ in one model but lose the phase-field structure of the target. We introduce Interface-Augmented Diffusion-Reaction (IADR), a neural operator that addresses both shortcomings: a target network with a diffusion-and-reaction (DR) structure preserves the phase-field structure of the Allen-Cahn equation, while a hypernetwork that maps $\varepsilon$ to the weights of this target network amortises the dependence on $\varepsilon$ across the range. A single IADR matches the per-$\varepsilon$ specialists on in-distribution data within the prescribed range, retains their cross-shape generalisation under both $\varepsilon$- and geometry-out-of-distribution shifts, and retains their compact DR target structure with millisecond-scale inference. We further establish a conditional $K$-step rollout error bound under consistency and stability assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Qinyi Zhang, Duanyu Feng, Yangshuai Wang, Hao Wang

item.title: Remotest Operator Control String-Averaging Methods in Feasibility-Seeking
item.description: arXiv:2611.30201v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The string-averaging (SA) method is a versatile algorithmic scheme for solving feasibility-seeking problems. It partitions the index set of all constraints into subsets of indices, called strings, allowing the user to apply operators successively along each string separately, and thus in parallel. The end-points of all such string operations are convexly combined to create the next iterate. Due to its flexible framework, SA is not restricted solely to this procedure; however, this characteristic applies only to the simultaneous step, while the sequential one is restricted to operator compositions. To permit alternative strategies in the latter, a novel algorithmic structure termed the Skeletal SA is introduced. Although its convergence is not established, it serves as a foundational "parent" structure that unveils unexamined SA algorithmic structures, as well as other known methods, obscured by standard compositions. To demonstrate the benefit of adopting the Skeletal SA framework over the standard SA scheme, we investigate a new approach, where instead of passing sequentially over each string via compositions, we employ a remotest-set-control-like strategy on every string by identifying the index of the operator farthest from the current iterate, and invoking it. This method favorably handles the common fixed point problem (CFPP), which requires finding a point within the intersection of finitely many constraint sets whose intersection is nonempty. Many iterative methods, including SA ones, have been proposed to solve the CFPP due to its importance in many scientific fields. However, remotest operator control SA (ROC-SA) methods have remained unexamined in this context.
item.dc:creator: Yair Censor, Ariel Nisenbaum, Simeon Reich

item.title: Cyclic changes of frame for designing non-retracing verification cases for numerical interface tracking
item.description: arXiv:2611.30464v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A forward-backward deformation test supplies an exact final interface, but retracing can allow errors from the two halves to cancel. We construct alternative tests by superposing a cyclic change of frame on the same base deformation. The frame returns to its starting pose, preserving the exact final phase and the deformation history up to rigid placement. A small returning translation can keep trajectories close to the retraced ones. A full rotation about a fixed centre or axis gives closed paths with nonzero winding for material labels that stay off that centre or axis. For incompressible base fields the transformed velocity is divergence-free. We construct discretely solenoidal face fluxes for geometric volume-of-fluid advection by circulating the transformed potential. In three TwoPhaseFlow benchmarks, with a shared time grid for each pair, a full-turn frame increased the final cell-average shape discrepancy in all 30 comparisons, with a median factor of 1.50. The fitted convergence exponent decreased in each of the six benchmark-reconstruction comparisons over the tested grids.
item.dc:creator: Dieter Bothe, Tomislav Mari\'c

item.title: Irreducible shallow tanh neural networks are a manifold
item.description: arXiv:2611.30553v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural networks (NNs) have been increasingly used as function approximators, motivating the study of the geometry of their function spaces. We study the set of functions represented by shallow neural networks with hyperbolic tangent activation, fixed input and output dimensions, and $n$ hidden neurons. In particular, we prove that the subset represented by irreducible networks in the sense of Sussmann (Neural Networks, 1992), i.e., networks with no redundant neurons, is a smooth embedded submanifold of the Sobolev spaces $\mathrm{W}^{\ell,p}$ on bounded sets for any $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p\in[1,+\infty]$. The key step is to show that if a sequence of networks converges in $\mathrm{W}^{\ell,p}$ to an irreducible network with the same number of hidden neurons, then the parameters of the approximating networks remain bounded. Finally, we show that this manifold has exactly $n+1$ connected components when both the input and output are scalar, and is connected otherwise.
item.dc:creator: Ivan Bioli, Isabella Carla Gonnella, Carlo Marcati, Federico Pichi

item.title: Fairness-optimized interlacing knots for even-degree periodic B-spline interpolation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30717v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Interpolating an ordered set of points by a B-spline curve is a fundamental operation in computer-aided geometric design. Most of the literature addresses open curves, where the Schoenberg--Whitney condition characterizes a nonsingular collocation matrix and averaging is the standard way to choose the knot vector. Periodic B-spline interpolation has received much less attention, and the open-curve algorithms cannot be transferred directly. No theoretical criterion is available for choosing the knots, and the few existing constructions, such as the shifting and energy methods, remain empirical, with neither a theoretical guarantee nor a supporting analysis. This paper addresses this gap for even degrees. We prove that for every even degree $p\ge2$ the periodic collocation matrix is nonsingular whenever the domain knots and the interpolation parameters interlace, in either of two admissible orderings, for arbitrarily nonuniform parameters. Rather than singling out one knot vector, this sufficient condition delimits an $n$-parameter family of admissible knot vectors and provides the theoretical foundation for knot selection that periodic interpolation has lacked. It also explains why the empirical shifting method is solvable, previously justified only by an incorrect diagonal-dominance argument. We then exploit the remaining freedom to place the knots by fairness optimization, which preserves admissibility at every iterate and leads to the methods Opt-R and Opt-L. On four closed shapes with irregularly distributed points these methods achieve a fairness comparable to the shifting and energy methods, improve on them in several cases, and offer guarantees that no empirical construction provides.
item.dc:creator: Shutao Tang, Zixuan Zhao

item.title: Quantum Approximation and Integration in Sobolev Spaces -- Low Smoothness
item.description: arXiv:2611.31000v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the complexity of approximation and integration in Sobolev spaces in the quantum setting of information-based complexity theory (IBC). Previous results have been obtained under the assumption that the embedding condition holds. Here we drop this assumption and use a quantum version of a previously developed stochastic discretization technique.
item.dc:creator: Stefan Heinrich

item.title: Accurate Products, Inaccurate Inverse: Emulated FP64 BLAS in Blocked Triangular Inversion
item.description: arXiv:2611.31030v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: FP64 emulation on integer tensor units now ships in cuBLAS and GEMMul8, and each emulated matrix product can be checked against an accuracy grade. We ask if a routine built from such products inherits their accuracy, and show that blocked triangular inversion, the core of LAPACK's inverse of a symmetric positive definite matrix, does not. Under fixed-precision emulation every product passes the grade-B error bound of Demmel et al., yet the inverse errs at 7.1e-2, against 2.0e-15 natively. The matrices are well conditioned after diagonal scaling, but the scaling spans 64 binades. The cause is one product, T = X22 L21, whose summed index carries both the diagonal scaling and its inverse, which a grade-B bound does not absorb. Computing those products natively restores native accuracy; leaving any one of them emulated does not. The pattern holds on four GPUs, and on real covariance matrices the fixed-precision routes lose up to about four orders of accuracy. Equilibration, a solve-based association and cuBLAS's automatic dynamic precision avoid the loss, and an exact error recurrence audits a completed run. On an RTX 4090 the fastest accurate emulated inversion takes 0.40 of cuSOLVER's time. Where each product's scaling falls decides if per-product accuracy carries over to a composite routine, and that is what builders of emulated libraries need to check.
item.dc:creator: Erzheng Zhang

item.title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
item.description: arXiv:2611.31033v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erd\H{o}s problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.
item.dc:creator: Mohit Tekriwal, Het Mankad, Naifeng Zhang, Keita Teranishi, Sahil Bhola, Daisuke Uchida, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Franz Franchetti, Karthik Duraisamy, Jeffrey Vetter, Yohann Dudouit

item.title: When Positivity Matters: Maximal Distance Integrals on Curves and Surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.31045v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How far apart, on average, can $n$ points in a set $A$ be? As $n\to\infty$ the answer is the $\textit{maximal energy}$ $M^{+}(A)$, the largest possible value of $\mathbb{E}|X-Y|$ when $X$ and $Y$ are independent random points of $A$ with a common distribution. If the distribution is allowed to carry negative mass, we obtain a second constant $M(A)\ge M^{+}(A)$. It is often far easier to compute: when a signed equilibrium measure exists, it is characterized by a $\textit{linear}$ potential equation, whereas the positive problem must also locate the support of the mass. This paper asks when positivity matters, that is, when $M^{+}(A)<M(A)$. For polygons and polyhedra the extremal mass sits on the vertices and closed forms abound. Even so, every hollow convex polygon has $M^{+}<M$, and a simple kite shows how a vertex can be forced out of the support. For smooth curves and surfaces the answer depends on the shape. Circles and spheres have $M^{+}=M$. The ellipse $x^2+4y^2=4$ has $M^{+}=M$ numerically, and we give its value to 50 digits. The ellipses $x^2+9y^2=9$ and $x^2+25y^2=25$ have $M^{+}<M$ numerically, with gaps in the support. For the ellipsoid $10x^2+15y^2+12z^2=15$, studied by Larcher, Schmid and Wolf, we compute 50 digits of $M$ and give strong numerical evidence that $M^{+}<M$. The extremal measure vanishes on two caps around the ends of the shortest axis. Proofs and numerical methods are collected in appendices.
item.dc:creator: Steven Finch

item.title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
item.description: arXiv:2611.31211v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Dovelos

item.title: Reduced Basis method for finite volume simulations of parabolic PDEs applied to porous media flows
item.description: arXiv:2406.07950v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the context of underground gas storage (of CO2 typically) in saline aquifers, numerical simulation is a highly valuable tool to evaluate the impact of the uncertainties of various model parameters and to optimize, e.g., injection-production scenarios. For this purpose, finite volume approximations of Darcy's parabolic model for flows in porous media are usually run many times, for many values of parameters like permeability and porosity, at costly computational efforts. We study the relevance of reduced basis methods as a way to lower the overall simulation cost of multi-point finite volume approximations to Darcy's parabolic model for flows in porous media for different values of the parameters such as permeability. We aim to quickly evaluate any linear form (or quantity of interest) of the pressure for many parameter values. To this end, we construct reduced bases by a standard POD-Greedy algorithm. Our POD-Greedy algorithm uses two new goal-oriented error estimators designed from a discrete space-time energy norm independent of the parameter. We provide some numerical experiments that validate the efficiency of the proposed estimators.
item.dc:creator: S{\'e}bastien Boyaval (MATHERIALS, LHSV), Guillaume Ench{\'e}ry (IFPEN), Baptiste Guilbery (MATHERIALS), Jana Tarhini (IFPEN), Quang Huy Tran (IFPEN)

item.title: Surface elevation errors in finite element Stokes models for glacier evolution
item.description: arXiv:2408.06470v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The primary data which determine the evolution of glaciation are the bedrock elevation and the surface mass balance. From this data, which we assume is defined over a fixed land region, the glacier's geometry solves a free boundary problem which balances the time derivative of the surface elevation, the surface velocity from the Stokes flow of the ice, and the surface mass balance rate. This problem can be posed in weak form as a variational inequality over a cone of admissible surface elevation functions, those which are above the bedrock topography. After some preparatory theory for the Stokes problem, we conjecture that the corresponding continuous-space, implicit time-step variational inequality problem is well-posed if the surface kinematical equation is appropriately regularized. This conjecture is supported by physical arguments and numerical evidence. We then prove a general theorem which bounds the numerical error made by finite element approximations of nonlinear-operator variational inequalities in Banach spaces. This bound is a sum of error terms of different types, special to variational inequalities. When it is applied to the implicit time-step glacier problem there are three terms in the bound: an error from discretizing the bed elevation primarily near the glacier margin, an error from numerically solving for the Stokes velocity, and finally a C\'ea-type best-approximation error for the finite element space representation of the surface elevation. The design of glacier models is then reconsidered based on this mostly a priori error analysis.
item.dc:creator: Ed Bueler

item.title: Lyapunov Exponent Bounds for Random Products of Relaxed Projections
item.description: arXiv:2503.09469v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current performance bounds for randomized iterated projections, such as the Kaczmarz method, are often considered tight under per-iteration analyses, yet they are notoriously loose in practice. We derive asymptotic performance bounds that narrow this theory-practice gap, leveraging a new technique for bounding the spectral radii of operators arising in the Lyapunov exponent analysis of randomized iterations. The asymptotic analysis also uncovers the previously unexplained role of relaxation in improving performance, thereby resolving an open problem posed by Strohmer and Vershynin in 2007.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Entezari, Arunava Banerjee

item.title: Finite element conformal complexes in three dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2508.01238v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops three-dimensional finite element conformal Hessian and conformal elasticity complexes through a local-bubble Bernstein-Gelfand-Gelfand (BGG) construction parameterized by smoothness vectors. These complexes incorporate higher-order differential operators, including the linearized Cotton-York operator, and require conformal tensor spaces (i.e., symmetric and traceless tensor spaces) with nontrivial smoothness and trace conditions. We apply the discrete BGG framework at the level of local bubble complexes parameterized by vertex, edge, and face smoothness vectors, together with geometric bubble decompositions and a reduction operation. This yields exact bubble complexes over explicit admissible regularity ranges, together with the face-bubble exactness needed to assemble families of global conforming complexes with varying vertex, edge, and face smoothness. The construction recovers known conformal Hessian and conformal elasticity complexes as particular choices, while producing broader smoothness-parameterized families, including new exact conformal elasticity complexes with strictly weaker interelement continuity. The resulting complexes provide structure-preserving finite element building blocks for applications in relativity, Cosserat elasticity, and fluid mechanics.
item.dc:creator: Xuehai Huang

item.title: Dynamical feedback control with operator learning for the Vlasov-Poisson system
item.description: arXiv:2509.23063v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To meet the demands of instantaneous control of instabilities over long time horizons in plasma fusion, we design a dynamic feedback control strategy for the Vlasov-Poisson system by constructing an operator that maps state perturbations to an external control field. In the first part of the paper, we propose learning such an operator using a neural network. Inspired by optimal control theory for linearized dynamics, we introduce a low-rank neural operator architecture and train it via adjoint state method. The resulting controller is effective at suppressing instabilities well beyond the training time horizon. To generalize control across varying initial data, we further introduce a novel cancellation-based control strategy that removes the destabilizing component of the electric field. This approach naturally defines an operator without requiring any training, ensures perturbation decay over infinite time, and demonstrates strong robustness under noisy feedback. Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of the method in both one- and multidimensional settings.
item.dc:creator: Jingcheng Lu, Li Wang, Jeff Calder

item.title: Flexible fixed-point iteration and its applications for nonsymmetric algebraic Riccati equations
item.description: arXiv:2509.25942v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we reveal the intrinsic Toeplitz structure in the unique stabilizing solution for nonsymmetric algebraic Riccati equations by employing a shift-involved fixed-point iteration, and propose an RADI-type method for computing this solution for large-scale equations of this type with sparse and low-rank structure by incorporating flexible shifts into the fixed-point iteration. We present a shift-selection strategy, termed Leja shifts, based on rational approximation theory, which is incorporated into the RADI-type method. We further discuss important implementation aspects for the method, such as low-rank factorization of residuals, implicit update of large-scale sparse matrices, real arithmetics with complex shifts, and related equations of other type. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency of both the proposed method and the introduced shift-selection strategy.
item.dc:creator: Zhen-Chen Guo, Xin Liang

item.title: Exploring the Scaling Crossover of Generalized Jeffreys-Type Law: Stochastic Modeling, Analysis, and High-Accuracy Numerical Computation
item.description: arXiv:2510.07930v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The generalized Jeffreys-type law is formulated as a multi-term time-fractional Jeffreys-type equation (MT-TFJE), whose dynamics exhibit rich scaling crossover phenomena associated with different diffusion mechanisms. In this work, we provide a microscopic stochastic interpretation of the MT-TFJE through a continuous-time random walk (CTRW) framework with a generalized waiting-time distribution, elucidating the physical mechanisms underlying the scaling crossover. Based on the Laplace-Volterra formulation and spectral analysis, we establish the well-posedness and stability of the MT-TFJE and derive Sobolev regularity estimates under appropriate assumptions on the initial data and source term. We further develop a high-accuracy numerical scheme, termed CIM-CLG, which combines a contour integral method for temporal approximation with the Chebyshev-Legendre Galerkin method for spatial discretization. The proposed method achieves exponential temporal convergence under the stated regularity of the governing equation, together with high-order spatial accuracy. The temporal approximation involves $\mathcal{O}(N)$ independent contour evaluations, where $N$ is the number of contour points, while the FFT-based transforms have a computational cost of $\mathcal{O}(M^n\log M)$ for spatial dimensions $n=1,2$, with $M$ denoting the number of modes per spatial dimension. The resulting algorithm is naturally parallelizable. Detailed implementation procedures and rigorous error estimates are presented. Extensive numerical experiments in one and two dimensions demonstrate the efficiency, accuracy, and robustness of the proposed method, providing a computationally effective framework for generalized nonlocal diffusion problems.
item.dc:creator: Fugui Ma

item.title: A Semi-Lagrangian Adaptive Rank (SLAR) Method for High-Dimensional Vlasov Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2510.24861v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We extend our previous work on a semi-Lagrangian adaptive rank (SLAR) integrator, in the finite difference framework for nonlinear Vlasov-Poisson systems, to the general high-order tensor setting. The proposed scheme retains the high-order accuracy of semi-Lagrangian methods, ensuring stability for large time steps and avoiding dimensional splitting errors. The primary contribution of this paper is the novel extension of the algorithm from the matrix to the high-dimensional tensor setting, which enables the simulation of Vlasov models in up to six dimensions. The key technical components include (1) a third-order high-dimensional polynomial reconstruction that scales as $O(d^2)$, providing a point-wise approximation of the solution at the foot of characteristics in a semi-Lagrangian scheme; (2) a recursive hierarchical adaptive cross approximation of high-order tensors in a hierarchical Tucker format, characterized by a tensor tree; (3) a low-complexity Poisson solver in the hierarchical Tucker format that leverages the FFT for efficiency. The computed adaptive rank kinetic solutions exhibit low-rank structures within branches of the tensor tree resulting in substantial computational savings in both storage and time. The resulting algorithm achieves a computational complexity of $O(d^4 N r^{3+\lceil\log_2d\rceil})$, where $N$ is the number of grid points per dimension, $d$ is the problem dimension, and $r$ is the maximum rank in the tensor tree, overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Through extensive numerical tests, we demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithm and highlight its ability to capture complex solution structures while maintaining a computational complexity that scales linearly with $N$.
item.dc:creator: Nanyi Zheng, William A. Sands, Daniel Hayes, Andrew J. Christlieb, Jing-Mei Qiu

item.title: Some error estimates for semidiscrete finite element approximations of stable solutions to mean field game systems
item.description: arXiv:2511.13352v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We derive a priori error estimates for semidiscrete finite element approximations of stable solutions to time-dependent mean field game systems with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Expressing solutions to the MFG system as zeros of a nonlinear abstract mapping, we show that the stability of solutions is equivalent to the invertibility of its differential. This characterization allows us to apply the Brezzi-Rappaz-Raviart approximation theorem in combination with discrete L^p maximal regularity estimates to prove existence of solutions to the semidiscrete MFG system and to derive the error estimate. Finally, for solutions satisfying sufficient regularity assumptions, we establish quasi-optimal error bounds, meaning the approximation achieves the best possible convergence rate when the solution has sufficient smoothness.
item.dc:creator: Jules Berry (L2S)

item.title: Global Recovery from Local Data: Interior Nudging for 2D Navier-Stokes equations in a Physical Domain
item.description: arXiv:2601.11831v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In many real-world applications of data assimilation (DA), the strategic placement of observers is crucial for effective and efficient forecasting. Motivated by practical constraints in sensor deployment, we show that global recovery of the flow field can be achieved using observations available only in a subregion of the domain, possibly far from the boundary. We focus on the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations posed in a bounded physical domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Building on the continuous data assimilation framework of Azouani, Olson, and Titi (2014), we rigorously prove that the assimilated solution converges globally to the true solution under suitable conditions on the nudging parameter, spatial resolution, and the geometry of the observation region, specifically, when the maximum distance from any point in the domain to the observational subregion is bounded by a constant multiple of \( \nu^{1/2} \) (in terms of scaling). Our computational results, conducted via finite element methods over complex geometries, support the theoretical findings and reveal even greater robustness in practice. Specifically, synchronization with the true solution is achieved even when the observational subregion lies farther from the rest of the domain than the theoretical threshold permits. Across all three tested scenarios, the local nudging algorithm performs comparably to full-domain assimilation, reaching global accuracy up to machine precision. Interestingly, observational data near the boundary are found to be largely uninformative. This demonstrates that full observability is not necessary: carefully chosen interior observations, even far from the boundary, can suffice.
item.dc:creator: Rui Fang, Ali Pakzad

item.title: Fast, High-Accuracy, Randomized Nullspace Computations for Tall Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2602.16797v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we develop RLOBPCG, an efficient method for computing a small number of singular triplets corresponding to the smallest singular values of large, tall matrices. The algorithm combines randomized preconditioner from the sketch-and-precondition techniques with the LOBPCG eigensolver: a small sketch is used to construct a high-quality preconditioner, and LOBPCG is run on the Gram matrix to refine the singular vector. Under the standard subspace embedding assumption and a modest singular value gap between the two smallest singular values, we prove that RLOBPCG converges geometrically to the minimum singular vector. In numerical experiments, RLOBPCG achieves near-optimal accuracy on matrices with up to $10^6$ rows, outperforming classical LOBPCG and Lanczos methods by a speedup of up to $12\times$ and maintaining robustness when other iterative methods fail to converge.
item.dc:creator: Ethan N. Epperly, Taejun Park, Yuji Nakatsukasa

item.title: Factorization and monotonicity methods for reconstructing an impenetrable obstacle in inverse biharmonic scattering
item.description: arXiv:2605.02802v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the recovery of an impenetrable obstacle with a Dirichlet or Neumann boundary condition from far-field measurements. The associated data-to-pattern operators are noninjective, because the biharmonic scattered fields can be decomposed into propagative and evanescent components. We derive new symmetric factorizations of the far-field operator and analyzie the middle operators on the closures of the ranges of the adjoint data-to-pattern operators to establish range identities. These identities yield factorization criteria for the support of the obstacle when the wavenumber is not an associated transmission eigenvalue. Furthermore, we derive monotonicity criteria without excluding transmission eigenvalues. Numerical experiments for Dirichlet obstacles illustrate the reconstruction methods and show their performance with noisy data and for wavenumbers near a clamped transmission eigenvalue.
item.dc:creator: Tielei Zhu, Zhihao Ge, Bangmin Wu, Dongwoo Sheen

item.title: An energy-decreasing algorithm for the finite element approximation of ferronematic equilibrium states and its numerical realization
item.description: arXiv:2605.11160v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop an energy-decreasing algorithm for the finite element approximation of two-dimensional ferronematic equilibrium states. The problem is formulated as the minimization of the harmonic energy of two two-dimensional vector fields, both with prescribed length, together with an additional nonlinear relation on the orientation of the two vectors. The finite element setting is based on piecewise continuous finite elements on a weakly acute triangulation. The numerical realization of the energy-decreasing algorithm employs a decomposition-coordination framework and a Uzawa-like iteration. Numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the computational performances of the algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Alexandre Ern, Ruma R. Maity

item.title: A high-order IMEX-DG solver for atmospheric dynamics: rotating tests on non-conforming meshes
item.description: arXiv:2605.29598v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a high-order implicit-explicit discontinuous Galerkin (IMEX-DG) solver for the compressible Euler equations that accounts for rotational effects within an atmospheric framework. Time integration follows a second-order additive Runge-Kutta scheme, treating stiff acoustic modes implicitly and advective terms explicitly. The solver is built on the deal.II finite element library, combining matrix-free operator evaluation, adaptive non-conforming mesh capabilities, and distributed-memory parallelism. The inclusion of rotation extends the framework to large-scale atmospheric dynamics, where the Coriolis force plays a central role in geostrophic balance. Its incorporation into a high-order matrix-free DG discretisation is, however, non-trivial, as it requires a careful formulation of the discrete rotational operator. Two alternative treatments of the rotational and gravitational source terms within the solution strategy, based on nonlinear fixed-point iterations, are therefore introduced and compared in terms of accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. A discrete analysis of the rotational operator is also carried out in order to derive a formulation suitable for efficient matrix-free implementation. The proposed formulation is verified through convergence studies on rotating inertia-gravity wave benchmarks and further assessed in fully three-dimensional simulations of stratified flow over orography on both uniform and adaptive meshes. The numerical results show that the rotating IMEX-DG framework has the expected accuracy and stability properties while correctly capturing the asymmetry and wave structures induced by rotation in large-scale atmospheric flows.
item.dc:creator: Letizia Bottani, Tommaso Benacchio, Giuseppe Orlando, Luca Bonaventura, Allan Peter Engsig-Karup

item.title: Residual-Weighted Randomized Jacobi: Sharpened Bounds via Residual Concentration and Asynchronous Extension
item.description: arXiv:2606.01232v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study randomized stationary methods for symmetric positive definite linear systems in which component $j$ is selected with probability proportional to $|r_j|^\ell$. This family interpolates between uniform sampling on the nonzero residual components ($\ell \to 0^+$) and Gauss--Southwell relaxation ($\ell \to \infty$). For $\ell = 2$ we sharpen the one-step analysis using the inverse participation ratio (IPR) of the residual, $\nu^2(r) = n\|r\|_4^4/\|r\|_2^4$, which is $1$ for a uniform residual and approaches $n$ as it concentrates. The resulting bound multiplies the guaranteed expected-progress coefficient of uniform sampling by the IPR (and the expected progress, for constant-diagonal $A$). We extend the analysis to asynchronous execution via the Avron--Druinsky--Gupta (ADG) framework, obtaining, under an a priori envelope on the IPR, an epoch-based reduction bound in which the IPR controls both the progress coefficient and the certified delay window. Synchronous runs on three structured problems and eight Matrix Market matrices support the sharpened bound, and shared-memory experiments show an IPR trajectory nearly insensitive to concurrency. There, committing a buffered residual value (consistent reads, the easier case for ADG) led to divergence at high concurrency on every problem, while re-reading the component at update time (inconsistent reads) diverged in a minority of runs on one problem. We conjecture a feedback-damping mechanism, test its predictions, and find that sufficiently small fixed steps and an adaptive IPR-driven step-size rule removed the instability in every run, at a cost in speed.
item.dc:creator: Evan Coleman

item.title: Cascading Smoothers for Multigrid
item.description: arXiv:2606.12577v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multigrid methods are among the most effective frameworks for solving large-scale sparse systems. However, achieving their hallmark linear scaling and rapid convergence crucially depends on an effective smoother algorithm, whose design is often highly problem-dependent. This paper develops a new approach, referred to as cascading smoothers due to their operation as an ordered sequence of single-step block-diagonal smoothers. Each level in the cascade is optimised to maximally damp the output of prior steps via a Frobenius norm minimisation of the corresponding error propagators. In particular, we develop an additive (resp., multiplicative) formulation analogous to Jacobi (resp., Gauss-Seidel). Applied within a standard multigrid V-cycle, we show they are remarkably effective across a wide array of problems, including finite difference, finite element, and discontinuous Galerkin discretisations applied to Poisson, elliptic interface, and Stokes systems as well as multiphase variants. In every case, cascading smoothers closely match or significantly outperform their optimally-damped classical counterparts, yet require no parameter tuning apart from a few discrete solver choices. Additionally, the approach is highly parallelisable and robust to geometric and operator complexities such as unstructured meshes and high-contrast coefficients.
item.dc:creator: Robert I. Saye

item.title: The least-squares RBF-PU method for linear elasticity in the diaphragm geometry
item.description: arXiv:2608.23718v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The human diaphragm is vital for respiration and its simulation can aid in further understanding complications arising in individuals that have been subjected to mechanical ventilation. The diaphragm is very thin and hence its numerical simulation poses a challenge for most numerical methods. In this paper, we compute the deformation of real diaphragm geometries, which are modelled as linear elastic, and are subject to realistic boundary conditions. The method used is the unfitted least-squares radial basis function partition of unity method. The patches used are cylindrical and refinement is performed along the thin direction of the diaphragm. Both the unfitted nature of the method as well as the refinement technique make this method particularly well suited to solve problems formulated in thin geometries. We derive a theoretical proof showing that the method converges with high order to the solution of a well-posed linear elasticity boundary value problem.

item.title: Stochastic Gradient Leimkuhler-Matthews Integrator with Second Order Discretization Error
item.description: arXiv:2610.24781v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) has a discretization error of first order in the step size $h$, even with the full gradient. We study the stochastic gradient Leimkuhler--Matthews (SGLM) integrator, which has the same cost as SGLD, one stochastic gradient per step, and reuses each Gaussian vector in consecutive steps. For a potential strongly convex outside a ball and a Lipschitz test function, we prove the bound $\mathcal O(\frac{1}{Nh} + \Sigma^2 h^2 + h^4 \log^2\frac1h)$ on the mean square error (MSE) of time averages of SGLM over $N$ steps, where $\Sigma$ bounds the variance of the gradient noise. The proof uses a modified class that absorbs the non-Markovian part of SGLM. The discretization error enters this bound as $h^4 \log^2\frac1h$ and the MSE bound of SGLD as $h^2$, while a larger batch reduces only the term $\Sigma^2 h^2$ in both bounds. In Bayesian logistic regression on MNIST, SGLM has a smaller estimated MSE than SGLD. The coefficient of $h$ in the numerical bias of SGLM is given explicitly by the covariance of the gradient noise and the continuous Poisson equation. The coefficient for SGLD contains in addition the Hessian of the potential, which comes from the discretization error.
item.dc:creator: Xuda Ye, Yuliang Wang, Guang Lin, Cindy Xiangrui Kong

item.title: A comparison of parallel iterative methods for ILU triangular solves
item.description: arXiv:2611.00552v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Exact triangular solves parallelise poorly, limited by the size and number of the level sets, so on GPUs the factors from incomplete LU (ILU) factorisations are often solved approximately with parallel iterative methods. We compare four such methods: a Jacobi method, an Incomplete Sparse Approximate Inverse (ISAI), GMRES polynomials, and AIRG, a reduction multigrid built on GMRES polynomials, for which we introduce a parallel coarse/fine splitting that bounds the diagonal dominance ratio of the fine-fine block. We test them with ILU(0) and ILU(1) factors of canonical PDE problems and 91 SuiteSparse/Matrix Market matrices, the latter on a single GPU. AIRG is the most robust on the PDE factors, with nearly flat iteration counts under refinement and no per-problem tuning, but has the largest setup and memory costs. GMRES polynomials are more robust than the Jacobi method at a similar cost. As the inner solve of an ILU preconditioner with tuned inner iteration counts, ISAI gives the largest median speedups over a hipSPARSE exact triangular solve (4.5$\times$ and 6.8$\times$ for ILU(0) and ILU(1)), though this was dominated by smaller problems; on the largest ILU(1) problems all four methods give similar median speedups of 2.0-2.6$\times$.
item.dc:creator: S. Dargaville, C. C. Pain

item.title: A virtual element exterior calculus framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.09813v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a unified virtual element framework for compatible polytopal discretizations of differential forms in arbitrary dimension and at arbitrary order. On general polytopal meshes, a central challenge is to construct de Rham subcomplexes and establish stability estimates with mesh-independent constants. We construct a trimmed complex of conforming virtual differential forms recursively from local Hodge--Laplace boundary value problems and obtain a complete subcomplex by imposing additional moment constraints. The local spaces of these two complexes contain the trimmed and complete polynomial differential forms, respectively, and admit unisolvent degrees of freedom from which polynomial projections can be computed. The canonical interpolants commute with the exterior derivative, and each virtual complex has cohomology isomorphic to that of the continuous de Rham complex. For both virtual complexes and in every form degree, we establish negative-norm inverse estimates and thereby prove a mesh-uniform equivalence between the $L^2$ norm and the scaled degree-of-freedom norm. Through the cochain isomorphisms induced by the degrees of freedom, these norm equivalences yield uniformly bounded liftings of fully discrete data into the corresponding continuous spaces, in particular for the Discrete de Rham method. We also derive canonical interpolation error estimates and discrete Poincar\'e inequalities. As an application, we obtain an inf-sup stable mixed Hodge--Laplace method with harmonic variables and optimal-order convergence under sufficient regularity.
item.dc:creator: Xiaojing Dong, Yibing Han, Yunqing Huang

item.title: An all-steps-at-once algorithm for time-domain wave propagation in heterogeneous and unbounded media
item.description: arXiv:2611.19288v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose, analyze, and implement a convolution quadrature (CQ) algorithm for transient acoustic waves in an unbounded medium consisting of a heterogeneous domain embedded in free space, where the wave speed may be spatially variable and discontinuous. Multistep CQ, applied to the time-domain solution operator, reduces the evolution problem to a family of Helmholtz problems with damped complex frequencies, which can be solved independently in parallel, all time steps at once. The frequency problems are discretized by an overlapping coupling of finite elements (FEM) on a polygonal/polyhedral domain containing the inhomogeneity, and boundary elements (BEM) on a smooth curve enclosed by that domain, in the region where the medium is homogeneous, which accounts exactly for the unbounded exterior. Neither discretization needs to conform to the geometry of the heterogeneous domain, nor to each other. For the resulting FEM--BEM coupling we prove bounds for the solution operators of the transformed problems that are explicit in the Laplace parameter and the wave speed. These bounds yield convergence of the time discretization for A-stable multistep schemes. We also prove explicit estimates on the exponential decay of the transformed solutions away from the heterogeneity, which show that the correction provided by the BEM part is small but relevant, and cheap to compute: a few GMRES iterations suffice, and the correction is needed only over a fixed range of weakly damped frequencies, beyond which it becomes negligible and can be dropped. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates in time and space and explore iterative (multigrid) methods for the interior FEM problems.
item.dc:creator: V. Dom\'{\i}nguez, M. Ganesh

item.title: A time-domain adversarial example demonstrating the failure of $H^1$ elements in $a$-$\phi$ electromagnetic simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.26546v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frequently, $H^1$ continuous finite elements are used in computational electromagnetics despite it being widely known that such an interpolation is not guaranteed to furnish reliable approximations of solutions to general initial/boundary value problems. It is mathematically more natural to use $H(\text{Curl})$ elements (edge elements) than $H^1$ elements, since the former form part of a discrete complex that respects the differential-geometric structure of Maxwell's equations while the latter do not. However, most work discussing the failure of $H^1$ elements for electromagnetics is esoteric and concrete examples demonstrating the clear advantage of edge elements are generally restricted to quasi-static, frequency-domain, or eigenvalue problems. In this work, we summarize essential facts regarding $H^1$ and $H(\text{Curl})$ elements and present a physically feasible yet intentionally adversarial time-domain eddy-current example demonstrating the failure of gauge-penalized $H^1$ elements in an $a$-$\phi$ formulation compared to explicit gauge-free mixed scalar/edge $H^1/H(\text{Curl})$ elements. The results indicate that edge elements can be used to furnish reasonable results for general loading conditions, whereas penalized $H^1$ elements fail (e.g., converge to an incorrect state) even with mesh refinement.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Carlson, Sanjay Govindjee

item.title: A Trust-Region Interior-Point Stochastic Sequential Quadratic Programming Method
item.description: arXiv:2603.10230v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we propose a trust-region interior-point stochastic sequential quadratic programming (TR-IP-SSQP) method for solving optimization problems with a stochastic objective and deterministic nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. In this setting, exact evaluations of the objective function and its gradient are unavailable, but their stochastic estimates can be constructed. In particular, at each iteration our method builds stochastic oracles whose estimates of the objective value and gradient satisfy proper adaptive accuracy conditions with a fixed probability. To handle inequality constraints, we adopt an interior-point method (IPM), in which the barrier parameter is taken from a prescribed decreasing sequence and is reduced once a stochastic stationarity test is passed. Under standard assumptions, we show that, almost surely, the KKT residual vanishes along the iterations at which the barrier parameter is reduced, and every limit point of these iterates is a KKT point. We implement the method on a subset of problems from the CUTEst test set, as well as on constrained logistic regression problems, to demonstrate its practical performance.
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Fang, Jihun Kim, Sen Na, James Demmel, Javad Lavaei

item.title: Sensor Placement for Tsunami Early Warning via Large-Scale Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design
item.description: arXiv:2604.08812v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Real-time tsunami early warning relies on distributed sensor networks to infer seismic sources and seafloor motion. Optimizing these networks via Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) is exceptionally challenging for systems governed by hyperbolic partial differential equations, which lack the spectral decay required by standard low-rank approximations. We present a scalable Bayesian OED framework for linear time-invariant systems. By reformulating the inverse problem in the data space, we transform OED into dense matrix subset selection. We propose a multi-GPU, Schur-complement-update-based, greedy algorithm that solves the OED problem using a pipelined approach that fully overlaps I/O with GPU computations. Our framework achieves near-perfect weak and strong scaling across hundreds of GPUs on Perlmutter and Frontier. Applied to the 2025 Gordon Bell Prize-winning digital twin for tsunami forecasting in the Cascadia Subduction Zone, we optimize a 175-sensor network, minimizing the uncertainty of a parameter field with over one billion degrees of freedom.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: SC26: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis, 2026, pp. 234-253
item.dc:creator: Sreeram Venkat, Stefan Henneking, Omar Ghattas

item.title: Well-Conditioned Oblivious Perturbations in Linear Space
item.description: arXiv:2604.23193v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Perturbing a deterministic $n$-dimensional matrix with small Gaussian noise is a cornerstone of smoothed analysis of algorithms [Spielman and Teng, JACM 2004], as it reduces the condition number of the input to $O(n)$, and with it the complexity of many matrix algorithms. However, when deployed algorithmically, these perturbations are expensive due to the cost of generating and storing $n^2$ Gaussian random variables. We propose a perturbation that requires generating and storing $O(n)$ random numbers in $O(\log n)$ bits of precision, and reduces the condition number of any deterministic matrix to $O(n)$, matching Gaussian perturbations. Our result takes a step towards derandomizing matrix perturbations in numerical linear algebra, and in particular, implies that we can solve an $n\times n$ linear system to within $\varepsilon$ backward error in $O(n^2\log(n)/\varepsilon)$ time using only $O(n\log n)$ random bits. In our construction, we introduce the concept of a pattern matrix, which is a dense deterministic matrix that maps all sparse vectors into dense vectors in a way that goes beyond the classical uncertainty principle of the Fourier transform. We combine this with a sparse perturbation whose entries are dependent and located in a non-uniform fashion. In order to analyze this construction, we develop new techniques for lower bounding the smallest singular value of a random matrix with dependent entries.
item.dc:creator: Shabarish Chenakkod, Micha{\l} Derezi\'nski, Xiaoyu Dong, Mark Rudelson

item.title: Characterization of stability radii for robustly asymptotically stable dissipative Hamiltonian differential-algebraic systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.13891v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study linear time-invariant dissipative Hamiltonian differential-algebraic systems. We characterize when the systems are robustly asymptotically stable and derive exact conditions and bounds when this property is lost under structure-preserving perturbations.
item.dc:creator: Peter Benner, Volker Mehrmann, Anshul Prajapati, Punit Sharma

item.title: Conformal tubular parameterization and toroidal bending of tube-like surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2605.16305v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tube-like surfaces are widely encountered in geometry processing, engineering structures, and medical anatomy, yet their intrinsic longitudinal and circumferential information is not well preserved by conventional planar annular or rectangular parameterization domains. In this work, we propose a new conformal parameterization framework for open tube-like surfaces with two boundary components. The proposed method first constructs a fixed-boundary tubular parameterization by cutting the input mesh, computing a disk-to-parallelogram quasi-conformal map, and lifting the result to a cylindrical surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$. To reduce residual distortion introduced near the cut seam, we further introduce a localized quasi-conformal correction scheme formulated on an annular domain, which improves conformality while leaving regions away from the seam unchanged. To handle noisy or irregular input boundaries, we also develop a free-boundary variant based on boundary extension and cycle-Laplacian smoothing, allowing the prescribed boundary constraints to be imposed on artificial outer rings rather than directly on the original surface. Finally, as an optional post-processing step, we derive two conformal toroidal bending maps that embed the tubular parameterization into toroidal geometries without altering its conformal structure. Experiments on synthetic tube meshes and real vascular surfaces demonstrate that the proposed framework produces low-distortion parameterizations, effectively mitigates seam-induced artifacts, improves robustness for boundary-noisy inputs, and provides flexible tubular and toroidal target domains for downstream surface processing tasks.
item.dc:creator: Shunyu Yao, Gary P. T. Choi

item.title: The Stability of the Backward Problem for Photoacoustic Imaging in Attenuating Media via Carleman Estimates
item.description: arXiv:2607.07244v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper investigates the backward problem in time for photoacoustic tomography (PAT) in attenuating media. It is well-established that photoacoustic imaging in attenuating media can be accurately modeled by spatial fractional-order damping. This inverse problem is ill-posed in the sense of Hadamard. In this work, we construct a novel class of Carleman estimates independent of spatial variables, and by virtue of these estimates, we establish conditional stability estimates for this problem for the first time. Building upon this, we propose a Tikhonov-type regularization functional and derive its associated adjoint system. Furthermore, leveraging the established conditional stability results, we derive the convergence rate of the proposed regularization approach. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our theoretical findings through extensive numerical experiments.
item.dc:creator: Qihang Chen, Zhiyuan Li, Song Xu

item.title: A structured quasi-Newton augmented Lagrangian algorithm for nonlinear least squares with linear and nonlinear constraints
item.description: arXiv:2607.11239v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present an algorithm for solving nonlinear least-squares problems subject to a mix of nonlinear constraints, linear equalities, and bounds. The nonlinear constraints are handled through an augmented Lagrangian reformulation of the objective, while the linear constraints are kept explicit. Each outer iteration therefore requires the approximate minimization of the augmented Lagrangian over a polyhedron, which we carry out with a gradient projection technique combined with a trust-region step computation. To capture the second-order information specific to the least-squares structure, we approximate the Hessian of the augmented Lagrangian by a Gauss--Newton term corrected by a structured quasi-Newton update, activated by a hybrid switching rule. The correction is built from a secant equation that we derive for the augmented Lagrangian itself. The outer iteration follows the augmented Lagrangian framework of Conn, Gould, Sartenaer and Toint for linearly constrained subproblems, for which we provide an explicit inner solver: a trust-region method whose Cauchy point is computed along nested faces of the polyhedron, without any projection onto it, and safeguarded by classical active-set devices, namely the release of bounds based on least-squares multiplier estimates and $\varepsilon$-active bounds. We prove that this inner solver satisfies the stopping rule required by the outer analysis, which yields global convergence of the overall method to a first-order critical point, and report numerical experiments. Our method outperforms an augmented Lagrangian solver built on the same outer update rules but without least-squares structure, and is competitive in computation time with a state-of-the-art solver for nonlinear programming.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Borie, Fabian Bastin, St\'ephane Dellacherie

item.title: Reference-free logged energy-oracle recovery for neural approximations of symmetric coercive variational problems: conforming Riesz reconstruction and archive-level selection
item.description: arXiv:2608.16473v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural PDE training yields a finite checkpoint archive, yet its logged energy errors are inaccessible without the exact solution, while loss-based selection does not necessarily recover the logged energy oracle. For admissible neural approximations of symmetric coercive variational problems, we introduce a reference-free selection rule based on minimizing a computable conforming Riesz monitor. The exact residual-energy identity and conforming projection make the monitor an unconditional lower bound converging monotonically to each logged energy error under nested conforming refinement; under saturation, hierarchical enrichment yields a computable upper estimate and hence a lower-upper bracket. A key finding is that archive selection is order-sensitive: unresolved checkpoint-dependent components can reverse the oracle-non-oracle ranking at finite resolution, so checkpointwise recovery alone is insufficient. For finite archives, we prove uniform recovery, yielding convergence to the logged-oracle error and, without saturation, logged-oracle selection at sufficiently fine auxiliary resolution. Under saturation, the bracket gives a computable near-oracle bound and certifies unique logged-oracle selection upon interval separation. We also bound logging-resolution loss and certify oracle inclusion over prescribed comparison trajectories. Experiments on diffusion and elasticity, including a non-manufactured perforated plate, demonstrate energy-scale calibration, oracle-level selection, and modest post-processing cost. This work frames neural checkpoint selection as an ordering problem, establishes projection-based reliability guarantees beyond checkpointwise error estimation and loss-error equivalence, and opens directions for variational loss design and more general selection theory.

item.title: Quasilinear multiplication in the Cayley-Dickson tower
item.description: arXiv:2609.11588v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Direct evaluation of the defining product of the Cayley-Dickson algebra $A_n$ of rank $N:=2^n$ requires a quadratic number of arithmetic operations. This paper gives a uniform bilinear algorithm that computes multiplication in $A_n$ over a unital commutative ring $R$ in which $2\in R^\times$ using $O(N\log N)$ arithmetic operations and $O(N)$ auxiliary storage, given $A_n$ is defined with doubling parameters that are units with square roots in a fixed commutative algebra finitely generated as an $R$-module admitting a linear surjection onto the base ring preserving the identity. These conditions are satisfied by every Cayley-Dickson tower over $\mathbb{R}$ and over finite fields of odd characteristic, where the tensor rank of multiplication in $A_n$ is at most $(36n-69)2^{n-3}+10$ for $n\ge4$. To the author's knowledge, this is the first uniform subquadratic algorithm for multiplication in $A_n$. In single-core benchmarks over $\mathbb{R}$, an open-source implementation in the library fastCD is approximately $17$ times faster than direct multiplication at $N=1024$.

item.title: High-fidelity simulation and reduced-order modeling of optical pumping in quantum devices
item.description: arXiv:2610.41778v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Predicting spin polarization and light attenuation in optically pumped atomic devices requires solving the coupled diffusive quantum master equation (DQME)--light system. Its nonlinearity, spatially nonlocal coupling, and physical admissibility constraints make high-fidelity numerical simulation challenging. We develop a structure-preserving high-fidelity solver that combines second-order finite differences for three-dimensional atomic diffusion, explicit pseudo-time marching for atomic populations, and an exponential integrator for light propagation. Under a derived time-step restriction, the solver preserves population normalization and nonnegativity, as well as the positivity and monotonic attenuation of the light intensity. Three complementary test cases based on an analytical reduction, asymptotic limits, and an analytical invariant are constructed to verify the solver. To accelerate repeated parameter queries, we eliminate the light field and construct a reduced-order model (ROM) using proper orthogonal decomposition and Galerkin projection of the resulting integro-differential formulation involving only atomic populations. An exact quadratic expansion of the spin-exchange term and discrete empirical interpolation of the optical-pumping term make the cost of evaluating the reduced operators independent of the full-order dimension. Numerical tests verify the solver and demonstrate ROM accuracy outside the training set. The GPU implementation completes simulations with millions of unknowns in minutes, while single-core ROM evaluations take seconds, achieving respective speedup factors exceeding 150 and 7000 relative to the single-core high-fidelity solver.

item.title: Learning observable propagation with sparse local moments
item.description: arXiv:2611.18448v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a unified framework for predicting local moment dynamics in high-dimensional many-body systems from short-time trajectories. Thanks to the locality of the dynamics, we construct the transition moment matrices by projecting the Markov operator onto low-order connected-cluster basis functions supported near the target observable. Exploiting the spatial decay of time-lagged correlations, {these matrices} can be approximated in sparse-plus-low-rank form using trajectory samples, with computational cost scaling linearly in the system dimension and the number of trajectories. The learning error can be further reduced by correcting the memory effect induced by the Galerkin projection. We numerically demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework in extrapolating the dynamics of various many-body systems, including Langevin and Glauber dynamics for classical systems as well as Lindblad dynamics for open quantum systems. For reversible local binary-spin dynamics, we establish volume-uniform $O(\varepsilon)$-$L^2(\pi)$ approximation bounds for local observable dynamics using connected-cluster spaces with neighborhood radius $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ and cluster order $O(\log^2(1/\varepsilon))$. We further establish error bounds for repeated one-step propagation using exact moment matrices and their sparse-plus-rank-one compressions, uniformly in the time step and number of iterations.

item.title: On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions
item.description: arXiv:2611.18511v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests.
